name: hexapoda
why: A modal hex editor is a niche but pleasant way into binary files; standout only in its modal, colourful approach, not deeply strange.

brief.what_it_is: Hexapoda is a terminal hex editor for binary files, described on its homepage as a colorful modal hex editor. It opens a file and shows its bytes, with each byte colored by its value. Editing is modal and selection-first, in the style of Kakoune and Helix. The homepage lists inspection of the selection as signed, unsigned, binary, fixed-point, UTF-8 and color. It can also search, mark offsets, and jump to offsets. Replacing and deleting bytes are supported; inserting bytes is not yet.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no explicit motivation. It presents hexapoda as a hex editor that borrows the modal, selection-first editing model of Helix and Kakoune, with colour to make byte values easier to read.
brief.how_it_works: Editing is selection-first: you select bytes, then act on them, as in Helix. Multiple selections are supported, and a selection can be split into #-byte chunks. The repeat action (bound to * by default) repeats an action a set number of times, using the primary register as the count, so the count can come from a value in the file. The homepage says hexapoda uses ijkl for cursor movement by default and that keybinds are configurable.

commands_seen.context: From the usage section: selects the word at 0x4 and yanks it, then goes to 0xc and selects that many words using v*e. Shows the repeat action using a value from the file as the count.

brief.install_notes: The homepage says nothing about installation beyond the Homebrew package. It mentions a config file for hjkl-style movement and configurable keybinds, but the page does not give the config path, format, or any first-run steps.
brief.standout: The repeat action takes its count from the primary register, so the file's own data can drive how many times an edit repeats. Colour-coding bytes by value is less common in terminal hex editors. Together with Helix-style selection-first modal editing, it is an unusual combination in this niche.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows no release date, changelog, or commit activity. I did not find a repository link on the page to check.
brief.caveats: Inserting bytes is not implemented; only replacing and deleting work. Diffing is listed as missing. The homepage does not list platforms or licence. The homepage says features are incomplete ('for the most part', 'for now'), so behaviour may change. The scout's note also flags the modal approach as the main draw, not something deeply strange.

entry.title: hexapoda
entry.tldr: A terminal hex editor that colours each byte by value and edits the way Helix and Kakoune do: select first, then act.
entry.deeper_look:
Hexapoda opens a binary file and shows its bytes, each coloured by its value. The colour helps you spot structure, such as runs of zeros, text and repeated patterns, without reading every number. The homepage calls it "a colorful modal hex editor".

Editing is modal and selection-first, "like Kakoune and Helix". You select bytes, then act on them. Multiple selections work, and a selection can be split into fixed-size chunks. You can search, mark offsets, jump to an offset, and undo or redo. Replacing and deleting bytes work. Inserting does not yet.

The most interesting idea is the repeat action, bound to `*` by default. Instead of typing a count, it takes the count from the primary register, so a value read out of the file can decide how many times an edit repeats. The homepage example yanks a word at 0x4, goes to 0xc and selects that many words with `v*e`. That fits how binary formats are built, with length fields that say how much data follows.

The `<C-space>` key inspects the current selection as signed, unsigned, binary, fixed-point, UTF-8 and colour. That makes it a handy way to learn how the same bytes read under different interpretations. The homepage gives no stated motivation beyond the modal model and the colour.

entry.whats_unique: Byte values are coloured, editing is selection-first like Helix, and the repeat count can come from data in the file itself. That combination is unusual among terminal hex editors.
entry.caveats: Inserting bytes is not implemented and diffing is missing. The homepage says features are incomplete and shows no release dates, so behaviour may change.
